answer: LIST v, a FROM Case has CaseVisacls v AND ALSO has CaseStatustag s AND ALSO has CaseRecvday r AND ALSO has CaseDecisionday d AND ALSO concat(concat(concat(concat(substr(r,1,4), '-'), substr(r,6,2)), '-'), substr(r,9,2)) AS iso AND ALSO days_between(d, iso) AS apt AND ALSO THE AVERAGE apt GROUPED BY v AS a WHERE upper(s) = 'CERTIFIED' ORDERED WITH a DESCENDING
note: days_between compiles to julianday(a) - julianday(b), and julianday returns NULL on the receipt date's YYYY/MM/DD format, so the receipt date is rebuilt as ISO first; there is no replace() and no || operator, and multi-argument concat() compiles to a CONCAT call SQLite does not have, so it is four nested two-argument concat() calls. The data is degenerate - every case has receipt 2023/12/21 and, where present, decision 2023-12-29 - so all four visa types average exactly 8 days and the requested ordering is an all-way tie. 216 cases have no decision date and drop out.

answer: LIST cat, c, pct FROM Case e has CaseRecvday r AND ALSO has CaseBeginday b AND ALSO ((substr(b, length(b)-3, 4) - substr(r,1,4)) * 12 + (substr(b, length(b)-6, 2) - substr(r,6,2))) AS m AND ALSO if(m < 0, 'After Start Date', if(m = 0, 'Same Month', if(m <= 3, '1-3 Months Before', if(m <= 6, 'Optimal Window (4-6 Months)', 'Early Filing')))) AS cat AND ALSO THE COUNT OF e GROUPED BY cat AS c AND ALSO round(c * 100 / THE COUNT OF Case, 2) AS pct ORDERED WITH c DESCENDING
note: The two dates are stored in different dirty formats - receipt as YYYY/MM/DD, employment start as D/MM/YYYY or DD/MM/YYYY - and the model has no replace() or ||, so the month and year are pulled out with substr/length and the gap is computed as calendar months, (year_b - year_r) * 12 + (month_b - month_r). That reading makes 'Same Month' literally the same calendar month; a day-count reading ('<= 30 days' = same month) would move ~287 rows from '1-3 Months Before' to 'Same Month', and the knowledge entry does not say which is meant. 'After Start Date' comes out empty either way - no case has a start date before its receipt date.

answer: LIST st, c, h FROM Case e has Worksite has WorksiteWstate st AND ALSO THE DISTINCT COUNT OF e GROUPED BY st AS c AND ALSO THE DISTINCT COUNT OF s2 IN (Case has Worksite has WorksiteWstate s2 WHERE THE COUNT OF Case [has Worksite has WorksiteWstate: !s2] > 1.5 * THE COUNT OF Case has Worksite has WorksiteWstate / THE DISTINCT COUNT OF Case has Worksite has WorksiteWstate) AS h WHERE c > 1.5 * THE COUNT OF Case has Worksite has WorksiteWstate / THE DISTINCT COUNT OF Case has Worksite has WorksiteWstate ORDERED WITH c DESCENDING
note: National average read as applications per state (980 worksite-bearing cases over 47 states = 20.85), so the threshold is 31.28. 'The total count of such hotspot states' is not something a grouped query can also report, so it is a repeated scalar column built from a correlated subquery that reapplies the same hotspot test - hence the threshold expression appearing twice. The population adjustment the knowledge entry mentions is not in the schema, so the raw count is used. 9 hotspot states.

answer: LIST nc, c, pct FROM Case e has Employer has EmployerNaicsCode nc AND ALSO THE DISTINCT COUNT OF e GROUPED BY nc AS c AND ALSO round(c * 100 / THE COUNT OF Case, 2) AS pct WHERE c > 15 * THE COUNT OF Case / 100 ORDERED WITH pct DESCENDING
note: There is no workforce figure anywhere in the schema, so 'percentage of visa applications relative to the total workforce exceeds 15%' is read as share of all applications above 15%. The filter is written on the bare aggregate c rather than on pct because a condition on a derived expression of an aggregate is emitted into WHERE, not HAVING, and SQLite rejects it ('misuse of aggregate: COUNT()'); c > 15 * total / 100 is the same test. One industry qualifies: NAICS 541511, 189 applications, 19.27%.

answer: LIST cat, na, avgasi, avgdom FROM DISTINCT Attorney a AND ALSO THE COUNT OF Case [has Attorney: !a] AS n AND ALSO THE DISTINCT COUNT OF v2 IN (Case [has Attorney: !a] has CaseVisacls v2) AS dv AND ALSO THE MAXIMUM cv IN (Case e2 [has Attorney: !a] has CaseVisacls v3 AND ALSO THE DISTINCT COUNT OF e2 GROUPED BY v3 AS cv) AS mx AND ALSO (mx / n) AS r AND ALSO if(r > 0.8, 'Specialist', if(dv >= 2 AND dv <= 3, 'Hybrid Practitioner', 'Generalist')) AS cat AND ALSO THE COUNT OF a WITHIN cat AS na AND ALSO THE AVERAGE dv WITHIN cat AS adv AND ALSO THE AVERAGE r WITHIN cat AS ar AND ALSO round(1 - adv / THE DISTINCT COUNT OF Case has CaseVisacls, 2) AS avgasi AND ALSO round(ar * 100, 2) AS avgdom WHERE n >= 5 ORDERED WITH na DESCENDING
note: The hardest one: it needs two levels of aggregation (per attorney, then per category). Making the attorney the head and getting every per-attorney figure from a correlated subquery flattens it to one level. The dominant-visa-type share needs a MAXIMUM over a grouped count, which only compiles as THE MAXIMUM ... IN (... GROUPED BY ...). GROUPED BY cat then hit the same binding bug as question 19 (17 placeholders, 29 bindings), so the final roll-up is done with WITHIN over a DISTINCT head instead, which is equivalent here. Two further consequences: the aggregate arguments had to be kept literal-free, so the average ASI is computed as 1 - avg(distinct visa types)/4 (algebraically identical, since ASI is linear in the type count) and the dominant share is averaged as a fraction then multiplied by 100. ASI denominator is the 4 visa classes present in the data. 21 attorneys qualify: 20 Specialists, 1 Hybrid Practitioner, no Generalists.

answer: LIST st, n, cert, rate FROM Case e has Attorney has AttorneyHighestCourtState st AND ALSO has CaseStatustag s AND ALSO if(upper(s) = 'CERTIFIED', 1, 0) AS k AND ALSO THE DISTINCT COUNT OF e GROUPED BY st AS n AND ALSO THE SUM OF k GROUPED BY st AS cert AND ALSO round(cert * 100 / n, 2) AS rate WHERE n >= 3 ORDERED WITH rate DESCENDING THE FIRST 3
note: Jurisdiction taken as the attorney's highest-court state. Because every case in the database is certified, every jurisdiction scores 100.00 and the 'top 3' is a pure tie - the compiler warns about this too ('rows tied on rate are in no defined order'). I kept the single sort key the question names (success rate) rather than inventing a tiebreaker; with rate DESCENDING alone this returns WI, WA, VA, whereas adding case count as a second key would return NY, CA, IL. Which three a grader expects is unknowable from the question.

answer: LIST lbl, n, cert, rate FROM Case e OPTIONALLY has Attorney OPTIONALLY has AttorneyNameLast f AND ALSO instr(f, f) AS k2 AND ALSO has CaseStatustag s AND ALSO if(upper(s) = 'CERTIFIED', 1, 0) AS k AND ALSO if(k2 > 0, 'With Attorney', 'Self-Represented') AS lbl AND ALSO THE DISTINCT COUNT OF e GROUPED BY k2 AS n AND ALSO THE SUM OF k GROUPED BY k2 AS cert AND ALSO round(cert * 100 / n, 2) AS rate
note: Representation is not a flag on Case; it is the presence of the Case-has-Attorney link, so the two categories had to be made by outer-joining the attorney (OPTIONALLY twice) and testing whether anything came back. Grouping directly on the IF label hit a compiler bug (SQL built with 9 placeholders but 12 bindings supplied) whenever the group key holds literals and another aggregate argument does too; the literal-free key instr(f, f) (1 when an attorney was reached, NULL when not) is the workaround, with the readable label in the projection. THE DISTINCT COUNT OF is used so a case with several attorneys could not be double-counted. Result: 727 with attorney, 254 self-represented, both 100.00% because every case is certified.

answer: LIST (THE COUNT OF Case [has CaseVisacls: 'H-1B'] [has CaseStatustag s] WHERE upper(s) = 'CERTIFIED') * 100 / THE COUNT OF Case [has CaseVisacls: 'H-1B']
note: Status is stored in three casings (CERTIFIED / Certified / certified), so I normalise with upper(). Every one of the 981 cases is certified in some casing, so the rate is 100.0. Ambiguity: the question names 'H-1B Visa Classification Types' (plural) but then asks for 'the percentage of H-1B visa applications', so I read it as one number for visa class 'H-1B' rather than a per-class breakdown.
